newsitem.title: FRANCE: Russia says NATO can't build in new member states.
newsitem.headline: Russia says NATO can't build in new member states.

text.p: Visiting Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov said on Tuesday the key outstanding issue holding up an agreement between NATO and his country was that the western alliance must agree not to build modern military facilities on the territories of future new member states.

Speaking after talks with French Prime Minister Alain Juppe and Foreign Minister Herve de Charette, he said Moscow's main concern about the eastward enlargement of NATO was the threat of "NATO infrastructure advancing towards Russia's borders".

"As of now, we have agreed to avoid the permanent deployment of NATO combat forces beyond the borders of the existing 16 member states. We have to agree on not creating infrastructure to enable the forward deployment of those forces," he said.
The United States has stressed it will not accept any deal that gives candidate states in central Europe second-class status.
Juppe said he hoped NATO and Russia could reach agreement on a new, cooperative relationship by the end of May so that the alliance's enlargement did not cause new fractures in Europe.
NATO plans to invite several former Communist Warsaw Pact states to join the alliance at a July summit in Madrid. The favourites are Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
Primakov stressed that a NATO-Russia agreement would not mean Moscow changed its negative view of the expansion of the Atlantic Alliance but was a way of limiting the consequences.
Juppe told reporters: "We are in favour of the enlargement of NATO provided...it does not reconstitute new fracture lines within Europe.
"I hope we will be able to move forward by the end of May," he said.

Primakov declined to be drawn on a signing date, saying it depended on whether the content of the agreement was satisfactory. But he said he hoped NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana would bring constructive proposals when he visits Moscow next Tuesday.

Juppe said France would support Moscow's accession to multilateral institutions such as the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, the World Trade Organisation and the Paris club of creditor nations "in step with the progress of economic reforms in Russia".
NATO sources said France was keen to host a mini-summit to sign a document enshrining a new cooperative relationship between the 16-nation western defence alliance and Russia.
The sources said U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin tentatively agreed to aim for a signing on May 27 "somewhere in Europe".
They said the venue might well depend on whether France and the United States settled a dispute over NATO's southern command in time for that date.

Primakov, who is due to meet President Jacques Chirac on Wednesday, said Russia shared France's grave concern at the extremely serious situation in the Middle East caused by a new Israeli settlement in Arab East Jerusalem and a surge of what he called terror attacks.
French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said the two sides had agreed to coordinate initiatives with the United States to try to revive Israeli-Palestinian peace negotiations.
